title: Ki Teitzei: the forgotten sheaf (Deuteronomy 24:19)
hook: a sheaf left behind by accident belongs to the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, the worker paid before sunset. Your line was pay today. Today, still in the fields, a commandment you can only keep by accident.

Harvest day, a long time ago. The reapers have been cutting grain since dawn, binding it into sheaves, stacking them on the cart. The light is going. Everyone's tired. The farmer takes one last look across the field, and there, at the far edge, is a sheaf someone missed. A whole bundle of grain, lying in the stubble. Every instinct says walk back and get it. It's yours. You grew it. And the Torah says: don't.
screen: `HARVEST, FROM DAWN TO DUSK.` → `ONE SHEAF MISSED.` → `DON'T GO BACK.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "When thou reapest thy harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go back to fetch it; it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow." The same goes for olives: don't beat the branches a second time. And grapes: don't go back over the vines. What's left belongs to the people who have no field. The Hebrew name for the forgotten sheaf is shichecha, from the word for forgetting. And here's the odd thing. Many commandments can be planned. This one can only be kept by accident. Leave a sheaf on purpose and it's a gift, a good one, but it isn't shichecha. Only what you truly forgot counts. The verse ends with a promise: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thy hands. Rashi, quoting the early midrash, notices how strange that is. Blessed for something you didn't mean to do? Yes, he says, and how much more for good you do on purpose. And if a coin falls out of your pocket and a poor person finds it and lives on it, you're blessed through it too. There's even a story in the Tosefta of a pious man who found he'd forgotten a sheaf, and was so happy to fulfill this commandment that he told his son to bring offerings of thanks. A mistake, turned into a gift.
screen: `DON'T GO BACK FOR IT.` · `SHICHECHA: THE FORGOTTEN ONE.` · `KEPT ONLY BY ACCIDENT.` · `THE DROPPED COIN.` · then, large: `FORGOTTEN BECOMES GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Think of something you lost or left behind lately that still stings a little: the umbrella on the train, the twenty that slipped out of your pocket. Instead of the sting, try the farmer's view: someone may have found it, and needed it. Let it go as a gift you didn't know you were giving.
Ki Teitzei. When you go out. The portion where a forgotten sheaf belongs to the stranger, the orphan and the widow.
Your line: forgotten becomes given. Even a dropped coin can feed someone. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The laws of the forgotten sheaf, the corner of the field and gleanings are set out in the Mishnah's tractate Peah, and some farmers in the land of Israel still observe them; elsewhere they are studied as the root of Jewish giving to the poor.

chat.says: How can forgetting something count as keeping a commandment?
options: Shichecha counts only if you truly forgot the sheaf; left on purpose, it's a gift, but not this commandment.
It can't; the rabbis said only sheaves left on purpose count, since a commandment needs a plan.
It counts only if you go back for it later and carry it to a poor family yourself, as a gift.
chat.meaning: The verse says don't go back for a forgotten sheaf; it's for the stranger, the orphan and the widow. Only what you truly forgot counts as shichecha.

shichecha.meaning: the forgotten sheaf, left for the poor

Rashi.meaning: a medieval commentator, here quoting the early midrash

midrash.meaning: early rabbinic teaching drawn from the Bible's verses

Tosefta.meaning: an early collection of rabbinic teachings, beside the Mishnah

notes: Deuteronomy 24:19 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify. The blessing clause is paraphrased in the voice, not quoted.
Rashi on 24:19 (from Sifrei): blessing even without intent; a sela dropped and found by a poor person; paraphrased.
Tosefta Peah 3:8: the pious man who forgot a sheaf and told his son to offer a bull as a burnt offering and a peace offering; confirm.
Whether gifts to the poor from the field apply outside the land of Israel today: generally not biblically; howItsDone says some farmers in Israel observe them.
